Mesillat Yesharim 12:3: And therefore, he necessarily needs thorough knowledge of the halachot, to know the branches of the commandments and how far they extend.
Mesillat Yesharim 12:4: And also because forgetfulness is common regarding these fine details, he will need constant reading of the books that explain these details, in order to renew their memory in his mind, and then he will certainly be aroused to fulfill them.
Mesillat Yesharim 12:5: And likewise, regarding character traits, he necessarily needs to read the ethical works of the early and later authors. For many times, even after a person has firmly resolved to be among the exacting and clean, it is possible for him to become guilty in particulars, because his knowledge of them had not yet reached that point.
Mesillat Yesharim 12:6: For no person is born wise, and it is impossible for him to know everything; but through reading such matters, he will be aroused regarding what he did not know, and will reflect upon what he had not previously grasped. And even regarding what he will not find in the books themselves — for when his mind is awakened to the matter, he goes on to consider all its aspects and discovers new insights from the source of truth.
Mesillat Yesharim 12:7: And indeed, the things that undermine this trait are all the things that undermine watchfulness, with the addition of a lack of proficiency in the knowledge of the laws or the ethical teachings, as I have written. And they have already said, of blessed memory (Avot 2:5): "nor is an ignorant person pious" — for whoever does not know cannot act. And so they said (Kiddushin 40b): great is study, for it leads to action.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:1:
An Explanation of the Trait of Abstinence (Perishut)
Abstinence is the beginning of piety. And you will see that everything we have explained up to now is what is required of a person in order to be righteous, and from here onward is what is required in order to be pious.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:2: It follows that abstinence stands in relation to piety as watchfulness stands in relation to alacrity: the one is in turning from evil, and the other is in doing good.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:3: Now, the general principle of abstinence is what they said, of blessed memory (Yevamot 20a): "sanctify yourself through that which is permitted to you" — and this is the very meaning of the word itself, perishut — that is, to separate and distance oneself from a thing; that is, to forbid oneself something permitted, with the intention thereby of not coming near the prohibition itself.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:4: The matter is this: anything from which harm could possibly arise — even though it does not presently cause harm, and all the more so if it is not actually evil — one should distance himself and separate from it.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:5: And reflect, and you will see that there are three levels here:
Mesillat Yesharim 13:7: And there are their fences, which are the decrees and safeguards that our Sages, of blessed memory, decreed upon all Israel.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:8: And there are the further distancings that are incumbent upon each individual person of abstinence to make for himself — to gather himself within his own bounds and build fences for himself — that is, to forgo even permissible things not forbidden to all of Israel, and to separate himself from them, so that he will be kept at a great distance from evil.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:9: And should you say: from where do we learn that we should go on adding to the prohibitions, when our Sages, of blessed memory, have said (Yerushalmi Nedarim 9:1): "Is it not enough for you what the Torah has forbidden, that you come to forbid upon yourself other things as well?" And indeed, whatever our Sages, of blessed memory, saw in their wisdom needed to be forbidden and made into a safeguard, they have already done; and what they left permissible was because they saw that it was fit to remain permissible and not forbidden —
Mesillat Yesharim 13:10: so why should we now invent new decrees which they did not see fit to decree? Moreover, there is no limit to such a matter, so that a person would end up desolate and afflicted, deriving no enjoyment from the world at all; and our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Yerushalmi Kiddushin 4:4): a person is destined to give judgment before the Omnipresent for everything his eyes saw and he did not wish to eat of it, even though it was permitted to him and he was able to — and they supported this with the verse (Ecclesiastes 2:10): "and whatever my eyes desired, I did not withhold from them."
Mesillat Yesharim 13:11: The answer is: abstinence is certainly necessary and required, and our Sages, of blessed memory, warned concerning it, which is what is said (Torat Kohanim): "You shall be holy" — "You shall be abstinent."
Mesillat Yesharim 13:12: They further said (Ta'anit 11a): whoever sits in a fast is called holy — how much more so a Nazirite.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:13: They further said (Pesikta): "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" (Proverbs 13:25) — this refers to Hezekiah, king of Judah, of whom they said that two bundles of vegetables and a litra of meat were brought up to him each day, and Israel mocked and said: this is a king?!
Mesillat Yesharim 13:14: They further said (Ketubot 104a), of our holy Rabbi, that at the time of his death he lifted his ten fingers and said, It is revealed and known before You that I have not enjoyed this world even so much as with my little finger.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:15: They further said (Tanna DeVei Eliyahu 26): before a person prays that words of Torah should enter his innards, he should pray that food and drink should not enter his innards in excess.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:16: Behold, all these statements teach explicitly the necessity of abstinence and the obligation to it. However, in any case we need to reconcile the statements that indicate the opposite.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:17: But the matter is that there are certainly many distinctions and fundamentals in this: there is an abstinence which we were commanded, and there is an abstinence against which we were warned not to fail into, this being what King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 7:16): "do not be overly righteous."
Mesillat Yesharim 13:18: Let us now explain the good abstinence. We shall say that since it has become clear to us that all the affairs of the world are trials for a person, as we have already written above and proven with evidence, and it has likewise become clear to us how great is man's weakness and how close his mind is drawn to evils, it must necessarily follow that whatever a person can manage to escape from these matters, it is proper for him to do so, in order to be better guarded from the evil that follows at their heels. For there is no worldly pleasure that does not draw some sin in its wake.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:19: By way of example: food and drink, when cleared of all dietary prohibitions, are permitted. However, filling the belly draws in its wake the casting off of the yoke of Heaven, and the drinking of wine draws in its wake lewdness and other evil things. All the more so, when a person accustoms himself to being satiated with food and drink, that if his usual habit is lacking even once, it will pain him and he will feel it greatly.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:20: And because of this, he finds himself immersing in the full force of business toil and the labor of acquisition, so that his table may be set according to his desire, and from there he is drawn on to injustice and theft, and from there to false oaths and all the other sins that follow, and he removes himself from service, from Torah, and from prayer.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:21: All of which he would have been spared, had he not, from the outset, drawn himself into these pleasures.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:22: And in this vein they said concerning the rebellious son (Sanhedrin 72a): the Torah anticipated his ultimate end, etc.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:23: And likewise, regarding the matter of lewdness, they said (Sotah 2a): whoever witnesses a sotah in her disgrace should make himself a Nazirite from wine.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:24: And you will see that this is a great stratagem for a person, in order to be saved from his inclination — for since, while he is engaged in the matter of the transgression itself, it is difficult for him to defeat it and subdue it, he must, while still far from it, keep himself far away, for then it will be difficult for the inclination to bring him near to it.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:25: Behold, marital relations with one's own wife are entirely permitted. However, they already instituted immersion for those who had a seminal emission, so that Torah scholars would not be found among their wives like roosters — for even though the act itself is permitted, it nevertheless implants this desire within a person, and from there it can lead on to what is forbidden, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 107a): there is a small organ in a man — satisfy it, and it is hungry; starve it, and it is satisfied.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:26: Moreover, even at the proper time and the fitting occasion, they said of Rabbi Eliezer (Nedarim 20b) that he would uncover a handbreadth and cover two handbreadths, and would resemble one seized by a demon, so as not to derive pleasure even at the time of his own pleasure.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:27: Regarding clothing and adornments, the Torah did not warn concerning their beauty or their design, but only that they should not contain a forbidden mixture, and that they should have tzitzit — and then all of them are permitted.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:28: However, who does not know that from wearing splendor and embroidery, pride follows, and lewdness too borders upon it — besides the envy, desire, and injustice that follow from anything precious that a person desires to attain. And they have already said, of blessed memory (Bereishit Rabbah 22): as soon as the inclination sees a person hanging on his heel, adjusting his clothes and curling his hair, it says: this one is mine.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:29: Strolling about and conversation, if not concerning a forbidden matter, are certainly, by the law of the Torah, permitted. However, how much neglect of Torah study follows from them, how much evil speech, how many falsehoods, how much frivolity! And it says (Proverbs 10:19): "In the multitude of words there wants not transgression."
Mesillat Yesharim 13:30: The general rule of the matter: since all the affairs of the world are nothing but immense dangers, how could one not praise whoever wishes to escape them, and whoever increases his distance from them?
Mesillat Yesharim 13:31: This is the matter of the good abstinence: that a person should take from the world, in whatever use he makes of it, only what he is compelled to by the natural necessity that binds him to it.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:32: This is what Rabbi praised himself for in the statement I mentioned — that he did not enjoy this world even so much as with his little finger, even though he was the prince of Israel, whose table was necessarily a table of kings, befitting the honor of his princedom — as they said, of blessed memory (Avodah Zarah 11a): "two nations are in your womb" (Genesis 25:23) — this refers to Rabbi and Antoninus, from whose table lettuce, cucumber, and radish were never absent, neither in the summer nor in the rainy season. And Hezekiah, king of Judah, likewise.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:33: And the other statements I have mentioned all confirm and teach that a person should abstain from everything that is a worldly pleasure, so as not to fall into its danger.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:34: And should you ask and say: if so, then, if this is a necessary and required matter, why did the Sages not decree it as they decreed the other fences and enactments they made? Behold, the answer is clear and simple: the Sages decreed a decree only if the majority of the community can uphold it, and the majority of the community cannot be pious; but it is enough for them to be righteous.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:35: But the remnant among the people who desire to merit closeness to Him, blessed be He, and to merit, through their own merit, drawing along with them the rest of the masses who depend on them — it is fitting for them to fulfill the standard of the pious, which the others cannot fulfill
